newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Asian businesses wary of Hanson - poll. [CORRECTED 05:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Asian businesses wary of Hanson - poll. [CORRECTED 05:50 GMT]

text.p: Many of Australia's Asian business partners say race row politician Pauline Hanson is damaging Australia overseas and view her as racist and anti-Asian, according to a newspaper poll published on Monday.

The poll in the Sydney Morning Herald newspaper, which surveyed 200 business leaders in Kuala Lumpur, Manila, Bangkok and Jakarta, found that six to seven percent (corrects from 16 percent) said they were now less likely to do business with Australian companies.
The poll, the first poll to gauge Asian leaders' attitudes to Hanson, asked them to comment on what they had heard about her. It found the biggest backlash was in Malaysia.

The survey also found that nearly a quarter of those questioned said they had heard of Hanson, compared with only five percent who said they had heard of Prime Minister John Howard, the newspaper said.
Hanson's name was recognised by 76 percent of respondents in Kuala Lumpur, 28 percent in Jakarta, 26 percent in Bangkok and 16 percent in Manila.
One comment from Kuala Lumpur said: "She is damaging for prospective Asians planning on going to Australia. The racist problem now makes people think twice about going there."

One Manila respondent said Hanson did not want to do business with Asia and that she should not be "closing doors to her neighbours like this" while a Bangkok respondent said she was anti-Asian and did not like Asian immigration.
When those aware of Hanson's views -- 37 percent of those surveyed -- were asked about her impact on tourism, 21 percent said they were less likely to travel to Australia.

But the survey found that 84 percent of the business leaders thought Australia was a "favourable" or "very favourable" country to do business with while 88 percent thought it was a "favourable" or "very favourable" holiday destination.

Of those who knew of Hanson's views, 44 percent said they had a negative influence on their attitudes, 53 percent said they had no effect, and three percent said they had a positive influence. The survey was carried out between July 8 and 18.
